subject: Art & Design
title: Leading and Tracking: Breathing Room for Text
description: A micro-lesson that makes Leading and Tracking: Breathing Room for Text usable.

hook.text: Cramped lines of text feel suffocating. Too much space feels disconnected. Leading controls this.

buildup.text: Leading (line-height) is the vertical space between baselines. Named after lead strips in printing presses.

discovery.text: Tracking (letter-spacing) adjusts space uniformly across all letters — unlike kerning's per-pair approach.

twist.text: Uppercase text needs extra tracking. Without it, capital letters look jammed together.

climax.text: The sweet spot for body text leading is 1.4-1.6× the font size. Tighter for headings, looser for body.

punchline.text: Space isn't empty. It's the rhythm between the notes.

quiz.question: What is the recommended line-height for body text?

details.summary: Leading (line spacing) controls the vertical distance between text lines, while tracking (letter spacing) controls horizontal spacing across all characters. Both create breathing room — too tight and text feels cramped and hard to read; too loose and lines disconnect, losing visual cohesion.
details.whyItMatters: Leading and tracking transform dense, unreadable text into comfortable reading experiences. These spacing controls are among the first adjustments professional typographers make.
takeaways: Leading controls vertical line spacing for readability
Tracking controls uniform horizontal letter spacing
Proper spacing transforms readability more than font choice

faq.question: What is the recommended leading for body text?
faq.answer: Generally 120-145% of the font size — so 12pt type would use 14.4-17.4pt leading. Longer line lengths need more leading so the eye can find the next line. Short line lengths (narrow columns) can use tighter leading. Sans-serif fonts often need slightly more leading than serifs.

faq.question: When should you increase tracking?
faq.answer: All-caps text benefits from increased tracking because uppercase letters have more uniform width, and extra space improves legibility. Very small text (captions, footnotes) is more legible with slightly increased tracking.
